background.definition: Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) is an acquired syndrome characterized by widespread intravascular activation of coagulation. It can be triggered by various stimuli and produce microvascular thrombosis with end organ damage. It may also present with clinically apparent thrombosis.

list.listitem: Occurs in 25% to 50% of patients with sepsis with a mortality rate of 40% to 80% in these patients.
Occurs in 1% of hospitalized patients.

A retrospective cohort study of more than 8,000 adult patients with DIC admitted to the Mayo Clinic from 2004 to 2010 found a decreasing incidence rate (26.2-18.6 per 100,000 person-years), but no change in case fatality rate.
See .
Massive inflammatory response leads to systemic activation of coagulation.

Activation of coagulation pathways and excessive thrombin generation leads to intravascular deposition of thrombin and microthrombi formation. This in turn causes microvascular endothelial damage with capillary leakage and shock, thrombosis, ischemia, and end organ failure.
Consumption of platelets and coagulation factors may lead to severe bleeding.
Most common signs and symptoms are evidence of both internal and external bleeding, ecchymoses, and thrombosis. C
A high index of suspicion is key to early DIC diagnosis. C
Monitor serial PT, PTT, platelet count, fibrinogen, fibrinogen degradation products, d-dimer. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Normal FDPs (can occasionally be mildly elevated)

list.listitem: DIC is a syndrome that can manifest with hemorrhage or thrombosis. The most critical factor is a high index of suspicion in the right clinical setting (see ).

In a series of 118 patients the most common presenting symptoms of DIC were: bleeding (64%), renal dysfunction (25%), CNS involvement (2%), hepatic dysfunction (19%), shock (14%), respiratory dysfunction (25%).
A thorough physical examination for ecchymosis, petechiae, oral and/or ophthalmic hemorrhage must be performed, as well as a comprehensive neurologic exam.
Fingers, toes, nose are the most commonly observed sites of decreased perfusion in patients with DIC.
When DIC is suspected clinically, order platelet count, fibrinogen, fibrinogen degradation product, d-dimer, and PT/PTT.
See for the International Society of Thrombosis and Haemostasis (ISTH) diagnostic algorithm for overt DIC.
Platelet count: decreased in DIC due to ongoing consumption. A platelet count less than 50,000 is seen in approximately 50% of patients.

Fibrinogen: a low fibrinogen can be found in DIC. It is important to measure this value serially in order to establish a trend. As an acute phase reactant it may remain elevated, particularly in patients with cancer, pregnancy, or inflammation.
Fibrinogen degradation products and D-dimers: these surrogate markers will be elevated in patients with ongoing DIC. High sensitivity for fibrinolysis but low specificity for etiology.
PT, PTT: usually prolonged but can be shortened or normal reflecting the ongoing consumption and stimulated production of clotting factors.
A scoring system has been created by the ISTH (). A score ≥5 is associated with sensitive (95%) and specific (95%) for DIC.
The diagnosis of DIC is based on a combination of the history, clinical presentation and laboratory abnormalities. Suspect DIC in patients with the conditions listed in .
See for guidelines regarding diagnosis and monitoring.
Serial monitoring of patients with DIC should include a detailed physical exam, evaluation for thrombosis and/or hemorrhage, daily PT/PTT, fibrinogen, FDP, d-dimer, and platelet count.
Identify and treat the underlying cause of DIC. C
In patients with a high risk of bleeding or frank bleeding, give FFP (10-15 mL/kg) and platelets (1-2 units per 10 kg per day). C
Antithrombin III and tissue pathway factor inhibitor are not effective. Activated protein C reduces mortality slightly but increases bleeding risk. B
The key to treating DIC is correction of the underlying disorder. The administration of platelets and coagulation factors is indicated in the bleeding patient with DIC.

The traditional dose of FFP is 10 to 15 mL/kg, which may be increased depending on the clinical severity. Transfuse platelets at 1 to 2 units per 10 kg per day if severe thrombocytopenia (less than 20,000) or moderate thromobcytopenia (less than 50,0000) and bleeding.

To stop the ongoing clotting process and eliminate further thrombosis, IV heparin has been used. Experimental studies demonstrate that heparin can interrupt the coagulation cascade. However, there are no clinical trials showing benefit or improved end organ outcomes. Do not use heparin if there is evidence of CNS hemorrhage.

A network meta-analysis of 1340 patients with sepsis-induced DIC in 9 studies found no significant differences in mortality or bleeding complications between antithrombin, thrombomodulin, heparin, protease inhibitors, and placebo.

Similarly, a Cochrane review found insufficient evidence for the efficacy of antithrombin III for critically ill patients, including those with sepsis and DIC. The authors found no mortality benefit, and bleeding rates may be higher with antithrombin III.
Trials using naturally occurring anticoagulants for DIC in sepsis:

The KyberSept trial was a double blind placebo controlled randomized trial of antithrombin III in patients with severe sepsis and shock. The intervention had no effect on all-cause mortality at 28 days.

The OPTIMIST trial of tissue pathway factor inhibitor in patients with severe sepsis did not demonstrate an effect on all-cause mortality in patients with severe sepsis and was associated with an increased risk of bleeding.
The PROWESS trial of activated protein C in patients with sepsis found a statistically significant 6.1% reduction in the mortality rate but was associated with an increase bleeding risk.

For patients with acute or chronic leukemia with DIC, a Cochrane review found insufficient evidence for the efficacy or safety of human activated protein C, recombinant human soluble thrombomodulin, tranexamic acid, and dermatan sulfate.

For pregnant or postpartum women with DIC, there is insufficient evidence for the efficacy or safety of hematological interventions. The authors of a Cochrane review found no RCTs evaluating heparin, danaparoid sodium, synthetic protease inhibitor, antithrombin, human recombinant activated protein C, recombinant soluble thrombomodulin, recombinant tissue factor pathway inhibitor, or recombinant activated factor VIIa.
The primary goal of management is to treat the underlying cause of DIC, i.e. antibiotics and fluid support for sepsis.
In one series of 148 patients, in hospital mortality was 32%. B
Patients with an increased DIC score (), elevated serum creatinine, and elevated level of fibrin have a worse prognosis. B

feature.caption: The International Society on Thrombosis and Haemostasis Scoring System for the Diagnosis of Overt DIC in Patients with an Underlying Disorder Associated with the Condition.
feature.feature_body:
Test Result Points
Platelet Count
>100,000 0
50 to 100,000 1
<50,000 2
Elevated Fibrin Related Marker (FDP, D-dimer)
No increase 0
Moderate increase 2
Strong increase 3
Prolonged PTT, in seconds
<3 0
>3 but <6 1
>6 2
Fibrinogen Level
>1.0 g/L 0
≤1 g/L 1
Total score (range 0 to 8 points):
Interpretation: If score is greater than or equal to 5, it strongly suggests overt DIC (95% sensitive and 95% specific). Repeat labs daily. If score is less than 5, it is suggestive but not affirmative of DIC; repeat labs in 1-2 days. Adapted from Taylor FB, Jr., Toh CH, Hoots WK, et al. Towards definition, clinical and laboratory criteria, and a scoring system for disseminated intravascular coagulation. Thromb Haemost 2001;86:1327–1330.
